name: Tretinoin
summary: A prescription skin medicine for acne; one cream version is also approved to soften fine wrinkles, blotchy pigment and roughness of facial skin.
what_it_is: Tretinoin, also called retinoic acid, is a prescription skin medicine sold as creams, gels and a liquid under names such as Retin-A. It is approved to treat acne, and a cream version (Renova) was approved to lessen fine wrinkles, blotchy pigment and roughness of facial skin in people who also follow a skin-care and sun-avoidance program. Taken by mouth, tretinoin causes birth defects in animals, so pregnancy is a key concern even with skin use.

evidence.why: It is FDA-approved for acne, and a cream version was approved for fine wrinkles and sun-related skin changes based on two 24-week trials in 315 people under 50; the wrinkle benefits were modest.

status_us.label: FDA-approved for acne; one cream for fine wrinkles
status_us.note: Tretinoin creams, gels and liquid are prescription drugs approved to treat acne (the microsphere gel for people 12 and older). Renova cream was approved as an add-on for fine wrinkles, blotchy pigment and roughness of facial skin; its label says it does not remove wrinkles, repair sun damage or restore younger skin.

benefits.claim: Treats acne vulgaris (approved use; the microsphere gel is approved for people 12 and older)

Modest improvement in fine wrinkles (24% versus 8% with a plain cream), blotchy pigment (38% versus 27%) and roughness (16% versus 10%) after 24 weeks in two trials of 315 people under 50 who also used sun protection (approved use); most of the effect fades after stopping

risks.risk: Skin irritation, such as redness, dryness, peeling, burning, stinging and itching, especially early on; nearly everyone in the wrinkle trials had some, and 4% stopped because of it
Acne can look worse in the first weeks of treatment
Sun sensitivity: skin burns more easily, and wind or cold can add to irritation
In hairless mice, tretinoin made ultraviolet light more likely to cause skin tumors; whether this applies to people is unknown

Pregnancy concerns: tretinoin taken by mouth causes malformations in animals, and skin application caused malformations in some rabbit studies; human studies have not shown a link with major birth defects, but the Renova label says not to use it in pregnancy
Temporary lightening or darkening of the skin with repeated use

avoid_if: Pregnant or trying to conceive (the Renova label says not to use it in pregnancy)
Eczema, or sunburned skin until it has healed (severe irritation)
Breastfeeding (no data on passage into milk; a clinician can advise)
interactions: Medicated or abrasive soaps and cleansers, and products with a lot of alcohol, astringents, spices or lime: more irritation
Products containing sulfur, resorcinol or salicylic acid: particular caution
Drugs that increase sun sensitivity, such as thiazide diuretics, tetracyclines and fluoroquinolones

labs.why: The labels reviewed call for no blood tests; their concerns are skin irritation, sun exposure and pregnancy.

studies.title: RENOVA (tretinoin cream): prescribing information
studies.people: 315 people under 50 with sun-damaged facial skin in two 24-week trials
studies.finding: Moderate improvement in fine wrinkling in 24% versus 8% on the plain cream base; the label says it does not eliminate wrinkles or reverse photoaging, was not shown to work in people over 50 or with darker skin, and most patients lose the effect after stopping.

studies.title: Tretinoin gel (microsphere): prescribing information
studies.finding: Approved for acne; skin irritation, burning, redness, peeling, dryness and itching were the most common side effects, and it can cause sun sensitivity.

ask_your_clinician: Which form suits my skin type, and how should I manage irritation?
I may become pregnant: should I use something else?
Can I use it with my other skin products, including acne washes and exfoliants?

sources.title: RETIN-A (tretinoin) cream, gel and liquid: prescribing information

notes_for_editor: Covers topical tretinoin only; oral tretinoin capsules were not researched. The labels conflict on animal data: the older Retin-A label says topical tretinoin was not teratogenic in rats and rabbits, while the 2025 microsphere gel label reports malformations in rabbit offspring after skin application; the entry reports the newer finding and the human data. The Retin-A copy on Drugs.com showed no revision date; an NDC List copy of the Retin-A cream label shows 'Rev. 11/16'. The Renova label opened is FDA's July 2000 version, which notes it may not be the latest; Renova's current marketing status was not checked, and the wrinkle-trial figures come from that label. The newer microsphere gel label (September 2025) uses the current pregnancy format and says human data have not shown a link with major birth defects, while the older Renova label says not to use it in pregnancy; both are reported. Over-the-counter retinoids and adapalene were out of scope. No independent review of tretinoin for photoaging was opened.
